claims.text: The material is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be produced by vacuum sintering.
Slow-cooled, vacuum-sintered equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr typically has a multiphase β-BCC1 + β-BCC2 + α-HCP microstructure.
Promoting SRO precipitate formation in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will reduce its lattice thermal conductivity.
Changing the cooling process can enhance the formation and volume fraction of SRO precipitates.
Changing the alloy chemistry can enhance the formation and volume fraction of SRO precipitates.
Slow cooling promotes SRO precipitates relative to water quenching.
The proposed comparison is to be performed at elevated temperatures of approximately 500–1000 °C under similar atmospheric conditions.
SRO precipitation produces associated nanoscale heterogeneities in the alloy microstructure.
SRO precipitates act as effective phonon-scattering centers.
Scattering by SRO precipitates shortens phonon mean free paths.
Shorter phonon mean free paths reduce the phononic contribution to thermal conductivity.
SRO-promoted samples will have measurably lower lattice thermal conductivity than samples without such precipitates.
Water-quenched equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is a metastable single β-BCC phase.
Water-quenched samples contain minimal SRO precipitates.
Water-quenched samples consequently have higher lattice thermal conductivity.
Electronic thermal conduction may complicate attribution of measured conductivity changes solely to SRO.
Interactions with interstitial oxygen may complicate attribution of measured conductivity changes solely to SRO.
The magnitude of the conductivity reduction is uncertain because of electron contributions and complex multiphase microstructures.

A comparison of otherwise identically prepared slow-cooled and water-quenched samples, with SRO quantified by TEM/XRD and lattice conductivity separated from electronic conductivity, can test the hypothesis.
